name: Swedish Empire
summary: Sweden’s “Great Power Era”, when it controlled much of the Baltic, until defeat in the Great Northern War.

knownFor.label: Vasa warship
knownFor.note: A royal warship that sank on its maiden voyage in Stockholm harbour; raised in 1961 and now a museum.

knownFor.label: Carolean soldiers
knownFor.note: Disciplined Swedish infantry of Charles XI and Charles XII, known for aggressive bayonet and pike charges.

knownFor.label: Light field artillery
knownFor.note: Gustavus Adolphus’ mobile regimental guns changed European warfare.

location.value: Sweden and Finland, plus Baltic provinces (Estonia, Livonia, Ingria), Swedish Pomerania, Bremen-Verden, and overseas New Sweden.
location.source: Wikipedia: Swedish Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Roberts, The Swedish Imperial Experience (1979)

terrain.value: Long Baltic coastlines, forests, lakes and the Gulf of Bothnia, which made the Baltic Sea the empire’s highway.

climate.value: Cold northern climate; the Little Ice Age shortened growing seasons.

resources.value: Iron and copper (Falun copper mine), timber, tar and grain from the Baltic provinces.

disasters.value: The Great Famine of 1695–97 killed a large share of Finland’s population.

population.value: About 2.5 million at its height (figure from the article’s later sections, not the infobox).

urbanisation.value: Stockholm grew into a capital city; Riga was the empire’s largest city.

disease.value: The plague of 1710–1713 struck Stockholm and the Baltic provinces during the Great Northern War.

migration.value: Settlers went to New Sweden on the Delaware River (1638–1655); Walloon ironworkers came to Sweden.

economicBase.value: Mining and export of copper and iron, farming, and Baltic trade tolls.

tradeRoutes.value: Baltic Sea trade, with tolls on Russian and Polish exports through Swedish-held ports.

wealth.value: No estimate is possible for this period.

moneyAndTax.value: The riksdaler and copper plate money; the first European banknotes (Stockholms Banco, 1661).

inequality.value: Nobles held much crown land until Charles XI’s “Great Reduction” took it back from the 1680s.

governmentType.value: A constitutional monarchy with the Riksdag (1611–1680 and 1719–21), and an absolute monarchy from 1680.
governmentType.source: Wikipedia: Swedish Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Roberts, The Swedish Imperial Experience (1979)

succession.value: Hereditary in the Vasa and then Palatinate dynasties; Christina abdicated in 1654.

institutions.value: The Instrument of Government (1634) set up a central bureaucracy; the Riksdag of the four Estates.
institutions.source: Wikipedia: Swedish Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Roberts, The Swedish Imperial Experience (1979)

stability.value: Stable at home, but nearly always at war abroad.

eliteConflict.value: Crown versus nobility over land: the “Reduction” of the 1680s returned estates to the crown.

armyAndTech.value: Gustavus Adolphus’ reforms: light mobile field artillery, combined arms and a conscripted national army (the allotment system).

majorWars.value: The Thirty Years’ War (Breitenfeld 1631), the Northern War of 1655–60, the Scanian War, and the Great Northern War (defeat at Poltava, 1709).
majorWars.source: Wikipedia: Swedish Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Roberts, The Swedish Imperial Experience (1979)

territoryChange.value: Took Scania and other lands from Denmark–Norway at the Treaty of Roskilde (1658); lost the Baltic provinces at Nystad (1721).
territoryChange.source: Wikipedia: Swedish Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Roberts, The Swedish Imperial Experience (1979)

alliancesRivals.value: Allied with France; rivals: Denmark–Norway, Russia, Poland–Lithuania and Brandenburg.
alliancesRivals.source: Wikipedia: Swedish Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Roberts, The Swedish Imperial Experience (1979)

inventions.value: Light regimental guns and the first banknotes in Europe (Stockholms Banco, 1661).

scienceEducation.value: Universities at Uppsala, Dorpat (Tartu, 1632) and Lund (1666).

openness.value: Recruited foreign officers and Dutch and Walloon experts in mining and finance.

religion.source: Wikipedia: Swedish Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Roberts, The Swedish Imperial Experience (1979)

languageWriting.value: Swedish, with Finnish, German and Baltic languages in the provinces.
languageWriting.source: Wikipedia: Swedish Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Roberts, The Swedish Imperial Experience (1979)

artsArchitecture.value: The warship Vasa (sank on its maiden voyage in 1628) and Baroque palaces such as Drottningholm.

socialStructure.value: Four estates in the Riksdag: nobles, clergy, burghers and peasants (free peasants had a voice, unusual in Europe).

sharedIdentity.value: Lutheran faith and the idea of Sweden as protector of Protestantism.

neighbours.value: Denmark–Norway, Russia, Poland–Lithuania, Brandenburg-Prussia and the Holy Roman Empire.
neighbours.source: Wikipedia: Swedish Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Roberts, The Swedish Imperial Experience (1979)

ideasReligions.value: Defended Protestantism in the Thirty Years’ War.

colonisation.value: New Sweden in North America (1638–1655) and a short-lived post on the Gold Coast.
colonisation.source: Wikipedia: Swedish Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Roberts, The Swedish Imperial Experience (1979)

riseSignals.value: Gustavus Adolphus (from 1611) reformed the army and government and entered the Thirty Years’ War.
riseSignals.source: Wikipedia: Swedish Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Roberts, The Swedish Imperial Experience (1979)

peakPeriod.value: Around 1658, after the Treaty of Roskilde gave Sweden its largest extent.
peakPeriod.source: Wikipedia: Swedish Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Roberts, The Swedish Imperial Experience (1979)

declineSignals.value: Overstretch against a coalition, defeat at Poltava (1709), plague and famine.
declineSignals.source: Wikipedia: Swedish Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Roberts, The Swedish Imperial Experience (1979)

outcome.value: The Treaty of Nystad (1721) ceded the Baltic provinces to Russia; Sweden lost great-power status (the “Age of Liberty” followed).
outcome.source: Wikipedia: Swedish Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Roberts, The Swedish Imperial Experience (1979)

overallCertainty.value: Good. Well documented by state archives; start and end dates are conventional (1611–1721).
